definition: Profit-driven criminal enterprise with a hierarchy and division of labor that runs ransomware, card fraud, and identity theft campaigns, usually well funded and skilled.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Cert Guide (Heuermann), Pearson – Chapter 5: Comparing and Contrasting Common Threat Actors and Motivations

definition: Threat actor who attacks systems, often critical infrastructure, to cause harm, fear, or disruption in support of a violent political or religious cause.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Cert Guide (Heuermann), Pearson – Chapter 5: Comparing and Contrasting Common Threat Actors and Motivations; SY0-801 objective 2.2

definition: Low-skill threat actor who runs ready-made programs and attack kits written by others, with little funding and limited understanding of how the attacks actually work.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 5: Compare and contrast common threat actors and motivations

definition: Threat actor who breaks into or disrupts systems, for example by defacing websites or leaking documents, to promote a social or political cause.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 5: Compare and contrast common threat actors and motivations

definition: Current or former employee, contractor, or partner who deliberately misuses authorized access to steal data or sabotage systems, often for money or revenge.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 5: Compare and contrast common threat actors and motivations

definition: Staff member who causes a security incident by mistake, such as clicking a phishing link or misconfiguring a system, with no harmful intent.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 5: Compare and contrast common threat actors and motivations; SY0-801 objective 2.2

definition: Rival business that attacks or spies on an organization to steal trade secrets, customer lists, or product plans and gain a market advantage.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Cert Guide (Heuermann), Pearson – Chapter 5: Comparing and Contrasting Common Threat Actors and Motivations

definition: Attacker group working for or funded by a government, with large budgets and top skills, that conducts espionage, sabotage, or cyber warfare against other countries.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 5: Compare and contrast common threat actors and motivations

definition: Long-running, stealthy intrusion campaign by a skilled, well-resourced group that gains a foothold in a chosen target and stays undetected for months to steal data.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 5: Compare and contrast common threat actors and motivations

definition: Person or group that intends to compromise the confidentiality, integrity, or availability of systems or data, for gain, for a cause, or for other reasons.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Cert Guide (Heuermann), Pearson – Chapter 5: Comparing and Contrasting Common Threat Actors and Motivations

definition: Attacker who operates from inside the organization, such as an employee or contractor, and can use existing access and knowledge of its systems.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 5: Compare and contrast common threat actors and motivations

definition: Attacker with no authorized access who operates from outside the organization and must rely on reconnaissance, exploits, or social engineering to get in.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 5: Compare and contrast common threat actors and motivations

definition: Attribute that measures the money, tools, infrastructure, and people an attacker can draw on, from a lone hobbyist's budget to a government's.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Cert Guide (Heuermann), Pearson – Chapter 5: Comparing and Contrasting Common Threat Actors and Motivations

definition: Attribute that measures an attacker's technical skill, from running downloaded tools to writing custom malware and exploiting flaws nobody else knows about.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 5: Compare and contrast common threat actors and motivations

definition: Motive of making money from an attack, for example through ransomware payments, card fraud, cryptocurrency theft, or selling stolen data.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 5: Compare and contrast common threat actors and motivations

definition: Motive of stealing trade secrets, designs, source code, or research so the attacker or its sponsor can copy them instead of developing them.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 5: Compare and contrast common threat actors and motivations

definition: Motive of forcing a victim to pay by threatening to leak stolen data, keep systems locked, or continue an attack unless demands are met.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 5: Compare and contrast common threat actors and motivations

definition: Motive of earning status and bragging rights in hacker communities by pulling off a visible attack and getting credit for it.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 5: Compare and contrast common threat actors and motivations

definition: Motive of exploring systems simply to see how they work or whether a break-in is possible, without a clear plan to profit or harm.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Cert Guide (Heuermann), Pearson – Chapter 5: Comparing and Contrasting Common Threat Actors and Motivations; SY0-801 objective 2.2

definition: Motive of a disgruntled employee, former partner, or other aggrieved person who attacks to punish an organization or individual for a perceived wrong.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 5: Compare and contrast common threat actors and motivations

definition: Motive of secretly gathering confidential government, military, or business information about a rival, typically through long-running hidden operations.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 5: Compare and contrast common threat actors and motivations

definition: Motive of shaping how a population or decision maker thinks or acts, for example by spreading disinformation or leaked material before an election.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Cert Guide (Heuermann), Pearson – Chapter 5: Comparing and Contrasting Common Threat Actors and Motivations; SY0-801 objective 2.2

definition: Motive of spreading panic and instability by knocking out services people depend on, such as power, transport, or communications, rather than for profit.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 5: Compare and contrast common threat actors and motivations

definition: Motive rooted in a set of social, religious, or moral convictions that drives attackers to target groups whose values or actions they oppose.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Cert Guide (Heuermann), Pearson – Chapter 5: Comparing and Contrasting Common Threat Actors and Motivations

definition: Motive of advancing or opposing a government, party, or law, for example by attacking officials' systems as a form of protest.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 5: Compare and contrast common threat actors and motivations

definition: Motive of attackers who see their actions as right, such as exposing flaws or wrongdoing so they get fixed, even when acting without permission.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 5: Compare and contrast common threat actors and motivations

definition: Continuously updated stream of attack data, such as malicious IP addresses, domains, and file hashes, that security tools can import to block or detect attacks.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 16: Explain various activities associated with vulnerability management

definition: Information about threats or targets collected from publicly available material such as websites, social media, public records, forums, and code repositories.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 16: Explain various activities associated with vulnerability management

definition: Curated attack data sold by a paid vendor under subscription, often enriched and filtered for a customer's industry, rather than freely published.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Cert Guide (Heuermann), Pearson – Chapter 16: Understanding Various Activities Associated with Vulnerability Management

definition: Member organization for one industry sector, such as finance or health care, where companies trade attack data and warnings with each other and with government.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 16: Explain various activities associated with vulnerability management

definition: Hidden part of the internet reached only through special software such as Tor, where stolen data, exploits, and attack tools are traded and analysts look for leaks.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Cert Guide (Heuermann), Pearson – Chapter 16: Understanding Various Activities Associated with Vulnerability Management

definition: Standardized JSON language for describing attack data, such as actors, campaigns, malware, and indicators, so organizations can share it in a common format.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 16: Explain various activities associated with vulnerability management

term: Trusted Automated Exchange of Indicator Information
definition: Protocol for automatically sharing STIX-formatted attack data between servers and clients over HTTPS, using a collection or a channel model.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 16: Explain various activities associated with vulnerability management

definition: Open framework that rates the severity of a software flaw from 0.0 to 10.0 using base, threat, and environmental metrics.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Cert Guide (Heuermann), Pearson – Chapter 16: Understanding Various Activities Associated with Vulnerability Management

definition: Public list, run by MITRE, that gives each publicly disclosed security flaw a unique identifier so vendors and tools can refer to the same issue.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Cert Guide (Heuermann), Pearson – Chapter 16: Understanding Various Activities Associated with Vulnerability Management

definition: US government repository, run by NIST, that enriches each catalogued security flaw with severity ratings, affected products, and fix references.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Cert Guide (Heuermann), Pearson – Chapter 17: Understanding Security Alerting and Monitoring Concepts and Tools

definition: Community-developed list of software and hardware flaw types, such as improper input validation, that describes root causes rather than individual bugs in products.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Cert Guide (Heuermann), Pearson – Chapter 16: Understanding Various Activities Associated with Vulnerability Management

definition: Ranking discovered flaws for remediation by severity, exploitability, asset value, and business impact so the most dangerous ones are fixed first.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 16: Explain various activities associated with vulnerability management

definition: Sorting discovered flaws into categories, such as application, operating system, configuration, or hardware weaknesses, to understand them and choose the right fix.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 16: Explain various activities associated with vulnerability management

definition: Basic cellular service for brief notes of up to 160 characters between phones, which attackers use to send fake alerts and links and to intercept one-time codes.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 6: Explain common threat vectors and attack surfaces

definition: Carrier messaging standard that upgrades phone texting with read receipts, typing indicators, rich media, and branded business messages; scammers also use it to send phishing texts.
source: Turn on RCS chats in Google Messages – Google Messages Help; RCS for Business – Google for Developers; SY0-801 objective 2.3

definition: Real-time chat apps such as WhatsApp or Signal, often end-to-end encrypted, through which attackers send malicious links and files or socially engineered lures.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 6: Explain common threat vectors and attack surfaces

definition: Shared workspace app such as Microsoft Teams or Slack where an attacker who joins or takes over an account can post malicious links or files that colleagues trust.
source: MITRE ATT&CK – T1566.003 Phishing: Spearphishing via Service; MITRE ATT&CK – T1534 Internal Spearphishing; SY0-801 objective 2.3

definition: Unsolicited bulk advertising or scam messages sent through chat apps instead of email, often carrying links to malicious sites.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Cert Guide (Heuermann), Pearson – Chapter 6: Understanding Common Threat Vectors and Attack Surfaces

definition: Two-dimensional square barcode that phone cameras decode into a link or text, which attackers print or email to send victims to malicious sites.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 14: Given a scenario, apply common security techniques to computing resources; SY0-801 objective 2.3

definition: Hidden code, links, or data concealed inside an image or other media file that runs or redirects the user when the file is opened or displayed.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 6: Explain common threat vectors and attack surfaces; SY0-801 objective 2.3

term: Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart
definition: Challenge-response test, such as reading distorted letters or picking matching pictures, that a website uses to keep automated bots away from logins and forms.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 7: Explain various types of vulnerabilities; SY0-801 objective 2.3

definition: Small script, usually written in VBA, stored inside an Office document that can run when the file is opened and download or launch malware.
source: CompTIA Security+ Practice Tests: Exam SY0-701 (Seidl), Sybex – Chapter 2: Domain 2.0: Threats, Vulnerabilities, and Mitigations; SY0-801 objective 2.3

definition: Cross-platform word processing file type that can carry embedded objects and links, which attackers send as attachments to exploit reader flaws.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Cert Guide (Heuermann), Pearson – Chapter 6: Understanding Common Threat Vectors and Attack Surfaces; SY0-801 objective 2.3

definition: Widely used fixed-layout file type, opened in readers such as Acrobat, that can contain scripts, links, and embedded files, making malicious attachments look like ordinary invoices.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Cert Guide (Heuermann), Pearson – Chapter 6: Understanding Common Threat Vectors and Attack Surfaces; SY0-801 objective 2.3

definition: Small add-on that extends Chrome, Edge, or Firefox and can read pages and form data, so a malicious or hijacked one can steal credentials.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 6: Explain common threat vectors and attack surfaces; SY0-801 objective 2.3

definition: Scripting language that runs inside web pages in the browser, which attackers abuse to inject malicious code, redirect users, or steal data from sessions.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 7: Explain various types of vulnerabilities

definition: Small text file a website stores in the browser to remember settings and logins; if stolen, it can let an attacker reuse the victim's signed-in session.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 8: Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity

definition: Unique value a web server issues after login to identify an authenticated user's ongoing visit, so whoever presents it can act as that user.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 8: Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity

definition: Router, switch, firewall, or other core network appliance whose compromise, often through outdated firmware or default settings, gives attackers control over traffic.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Cert Guide (Heuermann), Pearson – Chapter 7: Understanding Various Types of Vulnerabilities; SY0-801 objective 2.3

definition: Software version of a firewall, router, or other network gear that runs as a guest on a hypervisor, sharing host hardware and needing the same hardening and updates.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Cert Guide (Heuermann), Pearson – Chapter 6: Understanding Common Threat Vectors and Attack Surfaces; SY0-801 objective 2.3

definition: Temporary symmetric key generated for one connection or exchange to encrypt its traffic, so capturing or cracking it exposes that exchange's data.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 14: Given a scenario, apply common security techniques to computing resources; SY0-801 objective 2.3

definition: Service that lets a user see and control another computer's graphical screen over the network, a common target for password guessing when exposed online.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 18: Given a scenario, modify enterprise capabilities to enhance security; SY0-801 objective 2.3

definition: Platform-independent remote control system that shares a computer's screen, keyboard, and mouse through the Remote Frame Buffer protocol, often protected only by a weak password.
source: RFC 6143 – The Remote Framebuffer Protocol; MITRE ATT&CK – T1021.005 Remote Services: VNC; SY0-801 objective 2.3

definition: Attack that compromises a trusted vendor, contractor, or product component in order to reach the many organizations that rely on it.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 6: Explain common threat vectors and attack surfaces

definition: Outside company that supplies goods or services and is given access to an organization's data, network, or systems, extending its attack surface.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 6: Explain common threat vectors and attack surfaces; SY0-801 objective 2.3

definition: Outside firm that remotely runs a client's IT operations, so one compromise of its tools or accounts can spread to all of its customers at once.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 6: Explain common threat vectors and attack surfaces

definition: Company that transports, stores, or delivers goods, whose systems or shipments attackers can target to tamper with hardware or disrupt deliveries.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Cert Guide (Heuermann), Pearson – Chapter 6: Understanding Common Threat Vectors and Attack Surfaces; SY0-801 objective 2.3

definition: Vendor that hosts a complete application in the cloud for subscribers and holds their data, so a breach or outage on its side affects every customer.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Cert Guide (Heuermann), Pearson – Chapter 7: Understanding Various Types of Vulnerabilities; SY0-801 objective 2.3

definition: Company that makes or sells physical devices and components, whose products can arrive with counterfeit parts, tampered firmware, or implanted backdoors.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Cert Guide (Heuermann), Pearson – Chapter 7: Understanding Various Types of Vulnerabilities

definition: Company that develops applications or code libraries whose compromised build or release process can deliver malicious code to every user of its products.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Cert Guide (Heuermann), Pearson – Chapter 7: Understanding Various Types of Vulnerabilities

definition: Attack technique that relies on the operating system's own administration utilities, such as PowerShell or WMI, instead of malware, so activity blends in with normal work.
source: CISA, NSA, FBI and partners – Identifying and Mitigating Living Off the Land Techniques (joint guidance, 2024); CISA – AA23-144A People's Republic of China State-Sponsored Cyber Actor Living off the Land to Evade Detection; SY0-801 objective 2.3

definition: Thumb-size storage stick or gadget loaded with code that runs when plugged in, often dropped in a lobby or parking lot so a curious employee connects it.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 6: Explain common threat vectors and attack surfaces

definition: Network-connected everyday devices such as cameras, sensors, smart printers, and thermostats, often shipped with weak defaults and rarely updated.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Cert Guide (Heuermann), Pearson – Chapter 14: Applying Common Security Techniques to Computing Resources

definition: Hardware and software that monitor and control physical processes and machinery, such as industrial control systems and SCADA in plants, utilities, and pipelines.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 18: Given a scenario, modify enterprise capabilities to enhance security; SY0-801 objective 2.3

definition: Slipping through a secured door right behind an authorized person without that person noticing or agreeing.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Cert Guide (Heuermann), Pearson – Chapter 2: Summarizing Fundamental Security Concepts

definition: Entering a secure area with an authorized person's knowing help, for example by asking an employee to hold the door while carrying boxes.
source: CompTIA Security+ Practice Tests: Exam SY0-701 (Seidl), Sybex – Chapter 2: Domain 2.0: Threats, Vulnerabilities, and Mitigations

definition: Watching a person from nearby or through a camera to capture passwords, PINs, or on-screen data as they type or read it.
source: CompTIA Security+ Practice Tests: Exam SY0-701 (Seidl), Sybex – Chapter 2: Domain 2.0: Threats, Vulnerabilities, and Mitigations

definition: Fitting a hidden reader over an ATM or payment terminal slot to copy magnetic stripe or chip data, often with a tiny camera to capture the PIN.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 8: Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity

definition: Getting into a building, room, or device by breaking it open, such as smashing a window, prying a door, or defeating a lock.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 8: Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity; SY0-801 objective 2.5

definition: Copying the signal of a contactless door credential with a nearby reader so a duplicate can open the same doors.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 8: Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity

definition: Small entry room with two interlocking doors where only one opens at a time, so each person can be checked and following someone in is stopped.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 2: Summarize fundamental security concepts

definition: Physical credential, often a contactless fob, that a door reader checks before unlocking; a lost, shared, or copied one lets the wrong person in.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 2: Summarize fundamental security concepts; SY0-801 objective 2.3

definition: Short-range wireless standard for personal area networks that pairs phones, headsets, and keyboards; left discoverable, it exposes devices to nearby attackers.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 6: Explain common threat vectors and attack surfaces

definition: Very short-range radio technology, working within a few centimeters, used for tap-to-pay and contactless badges and open to nearby eavesdropping and relay.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 14: Given a scenario, apply common security techniques to computing resources

definition: Electromagnetic signals used by wireless networks, badges, and remote controls, which attackers can capture, replay, or jam from a distance.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 8: Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity; SY0-801 objective 2.3

definition: Sending unsolicited messages or contact cards to nearby discoverable Bluetooth devices, mostly annoying rather than harmful.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 14: Given a scenario, apply common security techniques to computing resources

definition: Stealing data such as contacts, messages, and calendars from a Bluetooth device without the owner's knowledge or permission.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 14: Given a scenario, apply common security techniques to computing resources

definition: Flooding a Wi-Fi or other airwave channel with noise or constant signals so legitimate devices cannot communicate, a form of denial of service.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 8: Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity

definition: Wireless base station connected to a corporate network without approval, bypassing security controls and giving outsiders a way in.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 8: Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity

definition: Fake wireless network that copies a legitimate network's name and settings to lure users into connecting so their traffic can be captured.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 8: Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity

definition: Hardware or software that has passed its vendor's end of support date, so newly found flaws will never receive fixes.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 6: Explain common threat vectors and attack surfaces

definition: Computer that still lacks available vendor fixes, leaving publicly known and often already exploited flaws open to attackers.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 7: Explain various types of vulnerabilities

definition: Outdated technology still in use because the business depends on it, though it runs old software and may not support modern security controls.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Cert Guide (Heuermann), Pearson – Chapter 7: Understanding Various Types of Vulnerabilities

definition: Endpoint that IT does not track or control centrally, so it misses updates, policy enforcement, and monitoring.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 7: Explain various types of vulnerabilities; SY0-801 objective 2.4

definition: Unauthorized hardware, such as a hidden wireless router or a small network implant, connected to the corporate network without approval.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 7: Explain various types of vulnerabilities; SY0-801 objective 2.4

definition: Systems, apps, or cloud services that staff adopt for work without the IT department's knowledge or approval, so they escape security review.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 5: Compare and contrast common threat actors and motivations

definition: Weakness caused by insecure settings, such as default passwords, open storage, needless services, or overly broad permissions, rather than by a flaw in the code.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 7: Explain various types of vulnerabilities

definition: Accounts, passwords, or keys left active after they are no longer needed, such as a departed worker's login, that attackers can quietly reuse.
source: CIS Critical Security Controls v8 – Safeguard 5.3 Disable Dormant Accounts; MITRE ATT&CK – T1078 Valid Accounts; SY0-801 objective 2.4

definition: Listening network endpoint of a running program that is reachable from outside, giving attackers a point to probe and exploit when it is not needed.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 6: Explain common threat vectors and attack surfaces

definition: Flaw where the outcome depends on the timing of two operations, so an attacker who acts between them can change data the program assumed was safe.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 7: Explain various types of vulnerabilities

definition: Moment when a program verifies a condition, such as a file's permissions or an account balance, before acting on it, opening a gap if things change afterward.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 7: Explain various types of vulnerabilities

definition: Moment when a program actually acts on a resource it validated earlier; if an attacker swapped the resource in between, the outdated validation is abused.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 7: Explain various types of vulnerabilities

definition: Tampered patch or new version, pushed through a trusted vendor's distribution channel, that installs attacker code on every system that accepts it.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Cert Guide (Heuermann), Pearson – Chapter 7: Understanding Various Types of Vulnerabilities

definition: Password, API key, or cryptographic key written directly into source code, scripts, or firmware, where anyone who reads the code or binary can find and reuse it.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Practice Tests & PBQs (Gorgotsias) – Chapter 3: Implementation; SY0-801 objective 2.4

definition: Coding flaw where failures are not caught safely, so the program crashes, fails open, or shows users stack traces and details that help attackers.
source: CompTIA Security+ Practice Tests: Exam SY0-701 (Seidl), Sybex – Chapter 2: Domain 2.0: Threats, Vulnerabilities, and Mitigations; SY0-801 objective 2.4

definition: Flaw that is unknown to the vendor or has no fix yet, so attackers can exploit it before any patch or detection signature exists.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 7: Explain various types of vulnerabilities

definition: Exploit that breaks out of a guest operating system to reach the hypervisor or other guests running on the same physical host.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 7: Explain various types of vulnerabilities

definition: Virtualization flaw where memory or storage given to one tenant or guest is reassigned to another without being wiped, exposing leftover data.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Cert Guide (Heuermann), Pearson – Chapter 7: Understanding Various Types of Vulnerabilities

definition: Weakness from outdated algorithms, short keys, poor random numbers, or bad key handling that lets attackers decrypt, forge, or tamper with protected data.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 7: Explain various types of vulnerabilities

definition: Installing a mobile app from outside the official app store, skipping its vetting, which can bring malware onto the device.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Cert Guide (Heuermann), Pearson – Chapter 7: Understanding Various Types of Vulnerabilities

definition: Removing a phone's built-in manufacturer restrictions to gain full administrator control, which also disables security protections and allows unvetted apps.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Cert Guide (Heuermann), Pearson – Chapter 7: Understanding Various Types of Vulnerabilities

definition: AI system trained on vast text collections to understand and write human-like replies; as an attack surface it can leak data, obey injected instructions, or emit unsafe output.
source: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025; NIST AI 600-1 Generative AI Profile; SY0-801 objective 2.4

definition: Openly accessible project on a hosting site such as GitHub, where leaked secrets, vulnerable dependencies, or poisoned packages can expose or infect anyone who uses it.
source: MITRE ATT&CK – T1593.003 Search Open Websites/Domains: Code Repositories; MITRE ATT&CK – T1195.001 Compromise Software Dependencies and Development Tools; SY0-801 objective 2.4

definition: Cloud blob container, such as an Amazon S3 one, left readable by anonymous internet users, often by mistake, so anyone can list or download its files.
source: MITRE ATT&CK – T1530 Data from Cloud Storage; Blocking public access to your Amazon S3 storage – AWS documentation; SY0-801 objective 2.4

definition: Malicious code that attaches itself to a host file or boot sector and spreads only when the infected file is run or shared by a user.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 8: Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity

definition: Self-contained malicious program that copies itself across networks by exploiting flaws, with no user action needed, often consuming bandwidth as it spreads.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 8: Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity

definition: Malicious program disguised as useful or legitimate software that tricks the user into installing it and then carries out hidden harmful actions.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 8: Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity

definition: Stealthy malware that gains administrator or kernel-level control and hides itself, its files, and its processes from the operating system and security tools.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 8: Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity

definition: Malicious code hidden in a legitimate program that stays inactive until a set date, event, or condition triggers its harmful action.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 8: Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity

definition: Malicious code that runs only in memory or through built-in tools such as PowerShell and writes nothing to disk, so file-based scanners miss it.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 8: Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity

definition: Malware that encrypts a victim's files or locks systems and demands payment, often in cryptocurrency, for the decryption key.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 8: Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity

definition: Malware that secretly monitors a user's browsing, location, and communications and sends the collected information to a third party.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 8: Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity

definition: Software that floods the user with unwanted advertisements, pop-ups, or browser redirects, often bundled with free programs to earn revenue from clicks.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 8: Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity

definition: Software or small hardware device that records every key pressed on a keyboard to capture passwords, card numbers, and messages.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 8: Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity

definition: Unneeded software preinstalled by a device maker or vendor that uses storage and memory and may add unpatched flaws to the system.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 8: Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity

definition: Software that is not clearly malicious but that the user likely did not mean to install, such as toolbars or trackers bundled with a download.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 8: Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity

definition: Malware hidden inside harmless-looking software that opens a backdoor, giving the attacker hands-on control of the infected computer over the network.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 8: Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity

definition: Flood of traffic or requests from many compromised machines at once, such as a botnet, that overwhelms a target so legitimate users cannot reach it.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 8: Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity

definition: Flooding attack that sends small requests with the victim's spoofed address to open servers, such as DNS or NTP, which send much larger replies to the victim.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 8: Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity

definition: Attack that forces two parties to negotiate an older, weaker version of an encryption standard or cipher, such as SSL instead of TLS, so the traffic can be broken.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 8: Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity

definition: Capturing and reading network traffic as it passes, with a tool such as Wireshark, to collect unencrypted passwords and data.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 8: Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity

definition: Faking an identifier, such as a source IP address, MAC address, email sender, or caller ID, so traffic appears to come from a trusted source.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 8: Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity

definition: Attack in which the intruder secretly sits between two communicating parties to intercept, read, or alter their traffic before relaying it.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 8: Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity

definition: Using a first compromised host as a stepping stone to reach and attack other systems deeper in the network that are not directly reachable.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 8: Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity

definition: Inserting forged records into a name resolver's stored answers so that later lookups for a legitimate site return an address the attacker controls.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 8: Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity

definition: Sending forged replies on a LAN that link the attacker's MAC address to the gateway's or another host's IP, so local traffic flows through the attacker.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 8: Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity

definition: Mass fraudulent message, usually email, that poses as a trusted organization to trick many recipients into clicking a link, opening an attachment, or giving up credentials.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 6: Explain common threat vectors and attack surfaces

definition: Fraudulent email crafted for a particular employee or team, using researched details such as names and projects, rather than sent to masses or to top executives.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 6: Explain common threat vectors and attack surfaces

definition: Fraudulent message aimed specifically at senior executives, such as the CEO or CFO, to steal high-value credentials or get large payments approved.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Cert Guide (Heuermann), Pearson – Chapter 6: Understanding Common Threat Vectors and Attack Surfaces

definition: Fraud delivered by text message that urges the recipient to tap a link, call a number, or reply with personal details, often posing as a bank or courier.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 6: Explain common threat vectors and attack surfaces

definition: Fraud carried out by phone call or voicemail, often with a spoofed caller ID, in which the caller poses as a bank, help desk, or official to extract information.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Cert Guide (Heuermann), Pearson – Chapter 6: Understanding Common Threat Vectors and Attack Surfaces

definition: Fraud that hides a malicious link in a two-dimensional barcode on a poster, parking meter, email, or text, so a victim's phone scan opens a fake site or installs malware.
source: FTC Consumer Advice – Scammers hide harmful links in QR codes to steal your information (2023); FBI IC3 – Cybercriminals Tampering with QR Codes to Steal Victim Funds (PSA, 2022); SY0-801 objective 2.5

definition: Pretending to be someone the target trusts, such as a help desk technician, executive, or police officer, to gain access or information.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 6: Explain common threat vectors and attack surfaces

definition: AI-generated or altered video, image, or voice that convincingly mimics a real person, used to trick staff into approving payments or sharing access.
source: NSA, FBI, and CISA – Contextualizing Deepfake Threats to Organizations (Cybersecurity Information Sheet, 2023); FBI IC3 – Criminals Use Generative Artificial Intelligence to Facilitate Financial Fraud (PSA, 2024); SY0-801 objective 2.5

definition: Inventing a believable story or reason for contact, such as an urgent IT problem, to persuade a victim to share information or take an action.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Cert Guide (Heuermann), Pearson – Chapter 6: Understanding Common Threat Vectors and Attack Surfaces

definition: Compromising a legitimate website that members of a target group often visit, so their browsers get infected when they go there.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 6: Explain common threat vectors and attack surfaces

definition: Registering a web address that differs from a popular one by a small typing mistake, so users who mistype it land on the attacker's site.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 6: Explain common threat vectors and attack surfaces

definition: Copying a well-known company's logos, style, and look-alike web addresses in fake emails or websites so victims trust them.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 6: Explain common threat vectors and attack surfaces

definition: Piece of forensic evidence, such as a known bad file signature, network address, or registry change, showing that a system has likely been breached.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 16: Explain various activities associated with vulnerability management

definition: Unique fingerprint of a file's contents that matches a known malware sample, letting tools flag the same file wherever it appears, even if renamed.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 8: Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity; SY0-801 objective 2.5

definition: Numeric network location known to host malware or command-and-control servers, whose appearance in firewall or proxy logs signals possible compromise.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 8: Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity; SY0-801 objective 2.5

definition: Internet name registered or hijacked for phishing or malware delivery, often newly created or look-alike, whose lookups in resolver logs point to infected hosts.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 8: Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity; SY0-801 objective 2.5

definition: Running program instance with an odd name, parent, path, or network activity, such as a word processor launching a command shell, that points to infection.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 8: Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity; SY0-801 objective 2.5

definition: Trace left on disk by attacker activity, such as dropped tools, odd items in temp folders, altered permissions, or prefetch records, found during an investigation.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 8: Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity; SY0-801 objective 2.5

definition: Recorded date and time of a file or event; values that are out of sequence, in the future, or changed to blend in reveal tampering.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 8: Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity; SY0-801 objective 2.5

definition: Human-readable characters found inside a binary or captured traffic, such as URLs, commands, or credentials, that reveals what a suspicious file or session does.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 8: Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity; SY0-801 objective 2.5

definition: Deleting, altering, or clearing records of system events to hide an intrusion, often shown by gaps, edits, or a wiped audit history.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Cert Guide (Heuermann), Pearson – Chapter 8: Understanding Indicators of Malicious Activity; SY0-801 objective 2.5

definition: Events recorded at unusual times, such as activity at 3 a.m. when the business is closed, suggesting someone is operating outside normal hours.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Cert Guide (Heuermann), Pearson – Chapter 8: Understanding Indicators of Malicious Activity

definition: Unexplained spikes in processor, memory, disk, or bandwidth use, which can point to malware, cryptomining, or data being exfiltrated.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Cert Guide (Heuermann), Pearson – Chapter 8: Understanding Indicators of Malicious Activity

definition: A user being shut out of a login after too many failed sign-ins, which, when the user did not cause it, suggests someone is guessing the password.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Cert Guide (Heuermann), Pearson – Chapter 8: Understanding Indicators of Malicious Activity

definition: Sign-ins to one account from distant locations within a time too short to get between them, suggesting the credentials are in someone else's hands.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Cert Guide (Heuermann), Pearson – Chapter 8: Understanding Indicators of Malicious Activity

definition: Same account logged in at once from several devices or places when the user normally has one, suggesting the account is shared or compromised.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Cert Guide (Heuermann), Pearson – Chapter 8: Understanding Indicators of Malicious Activity

definition: Security tools stopping access to sites, files, or downloads, where a surge of such denials can show malware trying to reach its servers or a user being lured.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Cert Guide (Heuermann), Pearson – Chapter 8: Understanding Indicators of Malicious Activity

definition: Users or admins suddenly unable to open files, systems, or accounts, which can signal ransomware encryption, changed passwords, or a denial-of-service attack.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Cert Guide (Heuermann), Pearson – Chapter 8: Understanding Indicators of Malicious Activity

definition: General category of attack that inserts untrusted input, such as commands or query code, into a program so it is executed as part of the program's own instructions.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 8: Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity

definition: Attack that enters crafted database commands into a web form or URL so the application runs them, letting the attacker read, change, or delete records.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 8: Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity

definition: Attack that plants malicious script in a trusted website, for example through a comment field, so it runs in other visitors' browsers and can steal their sessions.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 7: Explain various types of vulnerabilities

definition: Attack that writes more data into a memory area than it can hold, overwriting nearby memory to crash the program or run the attacker's code.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 8: Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity

definition: Attack that uses sequences such as ../ in a file name request to climb out of the web root and read files the server should not expose.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 8: Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity

definition: Attack that tricks a logged-in user's browser into sending an unwanted request, such as a fund transfer, to a site that trusts that browser's session.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 8: Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity

definition: Attack that makes a vulnerable server send requests on the attacker's behalf to internal systems or cloud metadata services it can reach but the attacker cannot.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 8: Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity

definition: Capturing valid network data, such as an authentication exchange or token, and sending it again later to repeat a transaction or gain access.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 8: Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity

definition: Exploiting a flaw or misconfiguration to gain higher access rights than were granted, such as a standard user becoming an administrator.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 8: Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity

definition: Taking over a user's authenticated web or AI chat connection by stealing or guessing its token, then acting as that user without having to log in.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 7: Explain various types of vulnerabilities; SY0-801 objective 2.6

definition: Trying one or a few common passwords against many different accounts, staying under the lockout limits that repeated guessing on one account would trigger.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 8: Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity

definition: Trying every possible password or key combination, usually with automated tools, until the right one is found.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 8: Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity

definition: Password guessing that works through a prepared wordlist of common passwords and real words, with variations, instead of every possible combination.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 8: Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity

definition: Discovering which account names are valid, for example from differing login error messages or response times, to build a target list for password attacks.
source: OWASP Web Security Testing Guide – Testing for Account Enumeration and Guessable User Account; CWE-204 Observable Response Discrepancy; SY0-801 objective 2.5

definition: Getting past the second sign-in step, for example by flooding a user with push approval requests, intercepting one-time codes, or stealing a session cookie issued after login.
source: MITRE ATT&CK – T1621 Multi-Factor Authentication Request Generation; MITRE ATT&CK – T1111 Multi-Factor Authentication Interception; MITRE ATT&CK – T1539 Steal Web Session Cookie; SY0-801 objective 2.5

definition: Reusing a captured password digest taken from memory to authenticate to other Windows systems without ever cracking the actual password.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 8: Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity

definition: Automated logins using username and password pairs leaked from other breaches, betting that users reuse the same login details across sites.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 8: Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity

definition: Altering an AI model's weights, settings, or components, for example through a compromised model file or supply chain, so it behaves the way an attacker wants.
source: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 – LLM03 Supply Chain and LLM04 Data and Model Poisoning; NIST AI 100-2 E2025 Adversarial Machine Learning; SY0-801 objective 2.6

definition: Corrupting the training, fine-tuning, or retrieval data of an AI system so the resulting model learns hidden backdoors, biases, or wrong behavior.
source: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 – LLM04 Data and Model Poisoning; NIST AI 100-2 E2025 Adversarial Machine Learning; SY0-801 objective 2.6

definition: Malicious instructions slipped into an AI system's input, typed directly or hidden in a web page, file, or email it reads, so it acts against its developer's intent.
source: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 – LLM01 Prompt Injection; NIST AI 100-2 E2025 Adversarial Machine Learning; SY0-801 objective 2.6

definition: Using role-play, hypothetical framing, or persistent rewording to talk an AI chatbot into ignoring its safety guardrails and producing content it is built to refuse.
source: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 – LLM01 Prompt Injection; NIST AI 100-2 E2025 Adversarial Machine Learning; SY0-801 objective 2.6

definition: Feeding a deployed AI model inputs with small, deliberate changes, such as altered pixels or reworded malware, so it misclassifies them, for example missing a threat.
source: NIST AI 100-2 E2025 Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations; OWASP Machine Learning Security Top 10 – ML01 Input Manipulation Attack; SY0-801 objective 2.6

definition: Running attacker-chosen commands on a system because an AI application passes model output or tool calls to an interpreter, shell, or plug-in without validating them.
source: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 – LLM05 Improper Output Handling and LLM06 Excessive Agency; SY0-801 objective 2.6

definition: Exposure of an organization's confidential information, such as source code or customer files, when staff paste it into outside AI tools or an AI reveals it to other users.
source: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 – LLM02 Sensitive Information Disclosure; NIST AI 600-1 Generative AI Profile; SY0-801 objective 2.6

definition: Systematic unfairness in an AI system's outputs, often inherited from unrepresentative training data, that favors or harms certain groups of people.
source: NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0); NIST AI 600-1 Generative AI Profile; SY0-801 objective 2.6

definition: Degree to which people can understand how and why an AI model reached a given output; when it is lacking, errors and manipulation are hard to spot or audit.
source: NIST IR 8312 Four Principles of Explainable Artificial Intelligence; NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0); SY0-801 objective 2.6

definition: Confident but false or made-up output from a generative AI model, such as invented facts, citations, or software package names.
source: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 – LLM09 Misinformation; NIST AI 600-1 Generative AI Profile; SY0-801 objective 2.6

definition: Risk that an AI system gathers, keeps, or infers personal details about individuals, or reveals them through memorized training data, without their consent.
source: NIST AI 600-1 Generative AI Profile; NIST AI 100-2 E2025 Adversarial Machine Learning; SY0-801 objective 2.6

definition: Questions of whether an AI use is fair, transparent, accountable, and respectful of people, for example around consent, job impact, and harmful or deceptive output.
source: NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0); NIST AI 600-1 Generative AI Profile; SY0-801 objective 2.6
